title: Largest Number
description: Arrange numbers to form the largest possible concatenation, using a custom a+b vs b+a comparator.

blocks.text: Given a list of non-negative integers nums, arrange them so their concatenation forms the largest possible number, and return that number as a string. Handle the special case where the largest arrangement would begin with a zero (meaning every number is zero), returning "0" in that case.

blocks.caption: A pairwise concatenation comparator decides the correct relative order of any two numbers.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (non-negative integers)"],["Output","A string representing the largest possible concatenation"],["Edge case","If every number is 0, the answer is \"0\", not \"000...0\""]]}

blocks.text: This is a custom-comparator sorting problem where the natural numeric or lexicographic order does NOT determine the correct arrangement. Instead, for any two numbers a and b, the correct relative order is decided by comparing the two possible concatenations, a+b versus b+a, and picking whichever forms the larger number.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This concatenation-comparison trick is a classic technique whenever "arrangement order" matters more than the individual values themselves, and it can be proven this pairwise rule extends correctly to a full sort via transitivity.

Picture number tiles being arranged in a row. For any two tiles, try placing them both ways, side by side, and see which concatenation reads as the bigger number. That ordering rule, applied consistently across all pairs, produces the arrangement that maximizes the overall number.

blocks.caption: Comparing both concatenation orders decides which tile should come first.

items: Convert every number to a string.
Sort using a comparator: a should come before b if (a+b) as a string is greater than (b+a).
Concatenate the sorted strings; if the result starts with '0', every number was 0, so return "0" instead.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Sorting all pairs this way produces the order [9,5,34,3,30], concatenating to "9534330", matching the expected output exactly.

A brute-force approach tries every permutation of the numbers, concatenating each and tracking the numerically largest result. This is correct but factorial in time, completely infeasible beyond very small inputs.

The concatenation-comparison rule (a+b vs b+a) captures exactly the right pairwise ordering, and this pairwise comparator is transitive, meaning a standard efficient sort using it as the comparator produces the guaranteed-optimal overall arrangement in one pass.

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Factorial growth makes this infeasible for anything beyond a handful of numbers.

Convert every number to a string, then sort using the comparator a+b vs b+a (as strings), placing the concatenation that reads as the bigger number first. Join the sorted strings; if the result begins with '0', return "0" instead (this only happens when every number is 0).

items: Sort with the concatenation comparator, O(n log n) comparisons, each comparison O(maxLength).
Concatenate and handle the all-zero edge case.

The a+b vs b+a concatenation comparator is a specific, provably-correct rule for "largest number from digits/numbers" style problems.
Always check for degenerate edge cases (here, an all-zero input) that a general sort-based solution might not handle automatically.

blocks.text: Largest Number is solved by converting each number to a string and sorting with a custom comparator that compares a+b against b+a, placing whichever concatenation is larger first. This pairwise rule extends correctly to a full sort, giving the optimal arrangement in O(n log n) time, with a small final check for the all-zero edge case.
